title: A Month After the First Indian-Heritage Major Champion, the U.S. Open Has Its Deepest-Ever Diaspora Field
excerpt: Aaron Rai arrives at Shinnecock Hills as a major winner, Akshay Bhatia as a ranked contender, and two qualifiers complete the largest contingent of golfers of Indian origin the championship has ever seen.
body:
The 126th U.S. Open began Thursday at the brutal, wind-scoured links of Shinnecock Hills on Long Island, and for the growing community of golf fans across the Indian diaspora, the marquee names this year are not only the usual suspects of Scottie Scheffler and Rory McIlroy. Teeing it up in the season's third major is the largest contingent of golfers of Indian origin the event has ever seen — led by a man who, just a month ago, rewrote the sport's history books.

**A barrier finally broken**

When Aaron Rai closed with a five-under 65 to win the PGA Championship at Aronimink in May, he became the first English golfer in 107 years to lift the Wanamaker Trophy. More significantly for millions watching from Punjab to New Jersey, he became the first player of Indian heritage to win a men's major championship. Born in Wolverhampton to a father whose family emigrated from India and a mother who arrived in England from Kenya, the 31-year-old has long spoken about how deeply his roots shape him. "Half of my upbringing is very British, but all of my close family is Indian origin," he has said. "That culture runs very deep even in British Asians."

Rai arrives at Shinnecock no longer as a curiosity but as a major champion, exempt into every big event on the calendar and carrying the quiet, two-gloved precision that has become his signature.



> **""Half of my upbringing is very British, but all of my close family is Indian origin," he has said."**


**The Californian who skipped college**

Sharing the spotlight is Akshay Bhatia, the 24-year-old from Northridge, California, whose parents Sonny and Renu raised him in Wake Forest, North Carolina. Bhatia famously turned professional straight out of high school, becoming the youngest American ever to play in a Walker Cup. Now a three-time PGA Tour winner who climbed to a career-high world ranking of 19 earlier this year, he has a U.S. Open pedigree, having finished tied for 16th in 2024. At Shinnecock he plays alongside Carlos Ortiz and Min Woo Lee in one of the more watchable early groupings.


![Long Island — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Montauk_01.jpg/3840px-Montauk_01.jpg)


**A deeper field than ever**

What makes this U.S. Open feel like a milestone for the diaspora is the depth behind the headliners. Manav Shah, the Bay Area-raised professional, earned his place through final qualifying, the gruelling 36-hole gauntlet known as "Golf's Longest Day." Sudarshan Yellamaraju, another qualifier, joins him in the field. Their presence means that on any given hole at Shinnecock this week, a leaderboard glance could turn up several South Asian surnames — something unthinkable in the sport a decade ago.

That progression is no accident. The trio of Rai, Bhatia and Sahith Theegala made headlines in 2024 when they appeared together at Tiger Woods' Hero World Challenge, openly discussing the role of Indian family values in their journeys. The pipeline they represent — built on first-generation immigrant sacrifice and a sport once seen as inaccessible to Indian families — is now bearing fruit at the highest level.

**Why Shinnecock matters**

Shinnecock Hills is one of American golf's original cathedrals, a founding member of the USGA and a course that has historically humbled the best in the world with its firm fairways, punishing fescue and relentless ocean wind. A strong week here, on a stage this demanding, would resonate far beyond the fairways. For Rai, victory would make him a two-time major champion in a single season. For Bhatia, a maiden major would confirm his arrival among the elite.

**What's next**

The opening round sets the tone, but the U.S. Open is a four-day war of attrition. The cut falls after Friday, and survival itself is an achievement on a course this severe. Whatever the final leaderboard reads on Sunday, the 2026 edition already marks a generational shift: golfers of Indian origin are no longer fringe entrants hoping to make a cut. They are major champions, ranked contenders and qualifiers who earned their spots the hard way — and the diaspora is watching every swing.

nri_angle: For the first time, golfers of Indian origin are competing at a U.S. Open not as curiosities but as major champions, ranked contenders and hard-earned qualifiers — a milestone moment for South Asian families across the US, UK and India who have embraced the sport.
author: Diaspora Desk
